A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same authors' study of RoPE and Transformer representations, despite substantial retitling and refocusing. Text, equations, figures, tables, and the complete v1 appendix are readable. V3 ends with references and contains no appendix.

before.justification: V1 reports original BookCorpus phase-shift experiments and synthetic aligned/misaligned sequence experiments on LLaMA models, including attention plots and extensive FFN activation results in Appendix 11.

after.justification: V3 reports original attention-pattern analyses on 500 BookCorpus sequences, with frequency, scale-sensitivity, reconstruction, and window-entropy results in Figures 1–3 and Tables 1–2.

M1.justification: The analytical procedure is substantially replaced. V1 perturbs extracted embeddings and probes FFN responses to sequence alignment; v3 Section 3 analyzes attention using DFT and db2 wavelet decomposition, coefficient comparisons across scales, and inverse reconstruction. This changes the study's analysis method, without introducing a new Transformer architecture.

E1.justification: BookCorpus remains, but v1's synthetic repeated-token versus alternating-token sequences and manually phase-rotated input scenarios disappear. V3 introduces token-subsampled natural-text scenarios at 0.5 and 0.25 scale. Removing the central synthetic alignment experiment substantially changes the tested input coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version benchmarks a proposed model or analytical algorithm against competing baseline methods. The pretrained models are subjects of analysis. ALiBi and T5 are added to v3's related work but are not evaluated as comparators.

E3.justification: V1 reports 1,000 BookCorpus samples of 200 tokens; v3 reports 500 variable-length sequences. The LLaMA-only study becomes seven reported model configurations across five families in Tables 1–2. New protocols measure spectral properties, reconstruction, sequence rescaling, and entropy over 16-, 32-, and 64-token windows, replacing attention-score and FFN-distribution measurements.

E4.justification: V1's rotation-frequency sensitivity study, aligned/misaligned FFN comparisons, activation distributions, and PCA analyses are removed. V3 adds head- and layer-level spectral analyses, scale-invariance tests, window-size entropy comparisons, and reconstruction checks. The diagnostic questions shift from phase interference to multi-resolution attention behavior.

E5.justification: V1 reports per-layer KS tests and t-tests with p-values in Tables 2, 6, and 10. These statistical tests disappear in v3, whose results provide point estimates without confidence intervals or significance tests. Its 'Uncertainty Analysis' concerns representation entropy, not uncertainty in estimated results. Neither version reports seeds or repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: The phase/attention findings and twelve FFN result tables in v1 are replaced by different spectral and wavelet results. For example, v1 Table 8 reports 41 versus 112 activation peaks for aligned versus misaligned LLaMA 3 inputs at layer 2; v3 Table 2 reports Mistral window entropies of 0.889, 0.877, and 0.877. These are different measurements, not comparable performance gains.

T1.justification: V1's eigenvalue analysis, cosine-based memory function, softmax expansion, and FFN harmonic derivations are largely removed. V3 introduces a wavelet framework with scale/translation functions, frame inequalities, multi-resolution expansions, and gradient-specialization and information-theoretic arguments in Section 6. The basic RoPE rotation matrix is retained, but the mathematical reasoning changes substantially.

C1.justification: V1's central claims concern RoPE-induced oscillations, nonlinear harmonic generation, and constructive/destructive phase interference. V3's abstract, introduction, and conclusion instead claim that attention heads develop wavelet-like multi-resolution representations that compensate for RoPE's limitations and become more sophisticated with model scale. This redefines the main contributions.

C2.justification: V1 interprets activation differences through interference, instability, and model-specific sensitivity to misalignment. V3 interprets spectral patterns as learned compensation, complementary scale specialization, and efficient information encoding. Its new limitations explicitly acknowledge inference-only analysis and that whether RoPE induces the behavior was not studied.

D1.justification: V1 specifies Colab Pro, an A100 GPU, and Hugging Face Transformers. V3 documents PyTorch and PyWavelets, A100/L4/T4 hardware, native tokenizers and attention masks, db2 wavelets, decomposition-level selection, and a 10^-10 numerical stabilization threshold. These substantially replace and expand the implementation information for the new analysis pipeline.

R1.justification: Research positioning shifts toward explaining compensation for RoPE limitations and connections to information theory. V3 adds Barbero et al. (2024), ALiBi, T5, and information-bottleneck/information-flow references, while removing earlier discussions and citations including Shaw, Transformer-XL, and Music Transformer. This exceeds a limited bibliography update.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, methodology, analysis, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. V1's progression through spectral properties, memory, attention, softmax, and FFNs is replaced by analysis procedures, implementation details, experiments, a wavelet framework, implications, and limitations. The extensive model-by-model appendix is removed.

P2.justification: V1's nine figures and twelve appendix tables are replaced by three new Pythia 12B visualizations and two compact cross-model tables. The displays change to local/global attention ratios, frequency-band distributions, and layerwise frequency responses. V3 also adopts a different page template and integrates all results into the two-column main text.

improvement.justification: V3 broadens the model analysis, improves implementation disclosure, and adds useful limitations. However, its central evidence has an unresolved inconsistency: Equation 7 defines scale sensitivity as 1 minus cosine similarity, while Section 5 interprets approximately 0.98 sensitivities in Table 1 as near-perfect correlations. Its learned-compensation claims also exceed the acknowledged inference-only evidence. V1 already contains reporting discrepancies, including its LLaMA 3 layer-10 t-statistic in Section 11.2 versus Table 6. These competing gains and evidential problems prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
